name: Fatima Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenbank, which is a co-op farm, about seventy hectares with two hundred ewes, some vegetables and a veg box scheme for families in town. There are six of us on the books and we all get a vote at the members' meeting, though the money's tight so the pay is low. My mornings are the sheep, checking feet and water and moving them between fields, and afternoons I'm usually in the polytunnels or packing boxes. On Thursdays I drive the van round the box deliveries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lambing, even though it's two weeks of hardly sleeping, and I like Thursdays because people say thank you at the door. What wears me out is the money. My partner Yusuf drives buses and we split rent on a flat above the bakery in the village, and between us we've got maybe two or three weeks saved. Every time the van needs tyres, it's a whole meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I can believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the members' meeting, good, now can we talk about the price of fertiliser instead. I might post something about how much electricity those data centres used for not much. People in the box scheme newsletter would probably like a line about real food grown by real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that's mostly good. I use one of those apps to identify blight on the tomato leaves now and then, and it saves me a phone call to the advisor. If that's all AI ever is, I'm happy with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep using the plant app when I'm not sure what I'm looking at. I'd keep pushing the co-op to raise the box price a little so we can pay ourselves better. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use an AI app now and then. When did you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last summer, after Tomasz, one of the other members, had been using it for a whole season and it turned out to be right about the blight. I don't jump on things. I wait till someone else has lost a crop finding out if it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what's your biggest worry for the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flock and the money, same as always. If the lamb price drops again we'll have to have the conversation about whether we can keep six people on. Nobody wants to be the one who says it.

S0.say: Good, now let's talk about real problems like the price of fertiliser. Those data centres used a lot of power for very little.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for me, and that's mostly fine. The plant app I use now and then is handy, and that's all I need AI to be.
S0.do: Carries on with sheep and vegetables, using the plant identification app when unsure. Pushes the co-op to raise the veg box price slightly so members can be paid a little more.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit smug about the hype fading.
S0.quote: I wait till someone else has lost a crop finding out if it works.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima's worries here are lamb prices and the co-op's tight budget, not technology. She describes her own approach clearly: she waits until a colleague has tested something for a season. The co-op structure gives her a vote, which shapes how she thinks about every later scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds more like what people actually expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should be the one that owns any new machines, not some company renting them to us. In public I'd argue for grants for small farms and co-ops so we don't get left behind by the big estates. I'd bring it to the members' meeting as a proper item.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big estates would get robots first and drive the prices down, and we'd have to follow or go under. Packing boxes and weeding are exactly the jobs a machine would take. If the co-op buys a weeding robot, one of the six of us goes, and we'd have to vote on who.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools more for the boring bits, the box orders and the newsletter, once I'd seen them work for the others. I'd push the co-op to apply for any grant going to share a robot with two other small farms. And I'd join the farmworkers' union, because the co-op can't fight for us on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a worry I can see coming, but it's not on me yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Greenbank, if one of you had to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Hannelore, she's fifty-eight and she does most of the packing. She's been there longer than anyone and she's got bad hands. I'd vote to keep her, but I don't know if the numbers would let us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools more. Wouldn't that help the machines take your job faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But if I don't learn them, I'm the one who's easy to cut. I'd rather be the person who knows how to set the thing up than the person it replaced.

S1.say: Co-ops and small farms should own the new machines, not rent them from companies. We need grants so small farms aren't left behind by the big estates.
S1.think: Big estates would automate first and drive prices down, forcing the co-op to follow. A weeding robot could mean one of the six members has to go, decided by a vote.
S1.do: Starts using AI tools more for orders and the newsletter once others have proven them. Pushes the co-op to apply for grants to share a robot with nearby farms. Joins the farmworkers' union.
S1.feel: Uneasy. She can see the worry coming but it isn't on her yet.
S1.quote: If the co-op buys a weeding robot, one of the six of us goes, and we'd have to vote on who.
S1.fieldNote: The co-op vote makes the threat personal in a new way: she might have to vote on who leaves. She defends learning the tools as self-protection rather than enthusiasm. She thinks of an older colleague first, which says a lot about her values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. We'd barely get through one more lambing before it hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud everywhere: this needs to be stopped or slowed until there's a plan for people. I'd want a basic income or something like it, and I'd say that online even though my uncle would argue with me in the family group. I'd go on whatever march the union organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Greenbank would close. A co-op of six people can't compete with an estate where robots do the lambing and the packing for nothing. We'd sell the ewes, we'd sell the van, and the bank would get the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, Yusuf and I would stop eating out and I'd cancel the gym I never go to. I'd go to my parents and ask whether we could move in with them if the farm closed, they've got a spare room since my brother left. And I'd be at the union meetings every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Yusuf's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I hadn't thought about until you asked. If robots can farm, they can drive a bus. So it's not one of us losing a job, it's both of us, and then the rent above the bakery is gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn something new in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I don't know what. The way I usually do things, I'd wait to see what worked for other people first, and there's no time for that here. That's what scares me most, that my careful way of doing things is too slow for this.

S2.say: This has to be slowed or stopped until there's a plan for people, like a basic income. I'd say it online and march with the union.
S2.think: The co-op would close because six people can't compete with robot-run estates. Her partner's bus job would likely go too, taking the rent with it.
S2.do: Cuts spending immediately, including eating out and the gym. Asks her parents about moving into their spare room. Attends union meetings weekly and joins marches.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake doing sums. Scared that her careful approach is too slow.
S2.quote: We'd sell the ewes, we'd sell the van, and the bank would get the rest.
S2.fieldNote: The follow-up about her partner's job changed her answer visibly; she hadn't connected the two before. Her habit of waiting until something is proven becomes a weakness with only two years. She still reaches first for collective action and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit of breathing room, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make sure farms like ours are part of it and not crushed by it. I'd lobby the council and the farming association for money for co-ops to buy shared machines, and I'd say so at the members' meeting. I'd want the union to push for a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is long enough to watch what works on other farms and then copy it, which is how I like to do things. If the co-op got a robot early and I was the one who learned to run it, maybe I'm the member who stays. It still ends with most of us gone, though, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put away fifty a month, which is what we can do if Yusuf picks up a Saturday shift. In the second year I'd sign up for a short course on farm machinery and robots, the agricultural college does evening ones. And I'd keep pushing the co-op to apply for a shared robot with the farms over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy anxious, which is better than lying-awake anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course cost, and could you manage it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last one I looked at was a few hundred for twelve evenings. We'd have to save for it, or I'd ask the co-op to pay half and I'd pay them back. I'd be the one asking for money at a meeting where we can't afford tyres, which isn't a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to see someone else try it first. In two years I'm just reacting, but with five I can watch Tomasz or the farms over the hill and learn from their mistakes. That's how I've always done things, so it suits me.

S3.say: We have five years to make sure farms like ours are part of the change, not crushed by it. Co-ops need money to buy shared machines and workers need a retraining fund.
S3.think: Five years gives her time to watch what works and copy it, which suits her. If she learns to run the co-op's robot she might be the member who stays, though most would still go.
S3.do: Saves about fifty a month with help from her partner's extra shift. Signs up for an evening course on farm robots in the second year, asking the co-op to cover half. Lobbies for co-op grants for shared machines.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, which feels better than the sleepless worry of the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I'd be the one asking for money at a meeting where we can't afford tyres, which isn't a nice feeling.
S3.fieldNote: The five years fit her habit of learning from others' mistakes, and she says so. Asking her poor co-op for course money makes her uncomfortable, a small, telling detail. She still expects most members to lose their place in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Maybe with kids by then, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to plan it properly, so the robots are owned by communities and co-ops, not just big companies. I'd want a law that shares out the gains. I'd keep saying it at the members' meetings and in the box scheme newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough time for me to move into something else on the farm side, like running and fixing the machines. I'd probably wait three or four years to see which machines won before I picked what to learn. Ten years is long enough that I'd stop being scared and start being annoyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving the fifty a month and do the machinery course around year three or four, once I knew which systems farms were actually buying. I'd stay at Greenbank and push for a shared robot that I'd help run. I'd keep up the union stuff, because the money still has to be shared out somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly hopeful, with a bit of worry about what Yusuf would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned maybe having kids. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. With two years I'd say no way, not with no job. With ten, I think we'd still want them, but we'd want to know where the money's coming from first, so maybe we'd wait a couple of years longer than we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the other members at the first meeting after hearing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's not panic and let's not sit still either. We've survived foot rot, two droughts and a bank manager called Gerhard, so we can survive a robot if we plan. Then I'd put it on the agenda every month.

S4.say: This is our chance to plan, so communities and co-ops own the robots, not just big companies. There should be a law that shares the gains.
S4.think: Ten years is enough for her to move into running and fixing the farm's machines. She'd wait a few years to see which systems win before choosing what to learn.
S4.do: Keeps saving about fifty a month and takes a machinery course around year three or four. Stays at the co-op and pushes for a shared robot she would help run. Stays active in the union.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, with some worry about her partner's job.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd stop being scared and start being annoyed.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima's fear turns to irritation and planning, and she said so herself. She'd delay retraining until the winners are clear, true to her steady approach. Kids came up unprompted, and she'd push them back rather than give up the idea.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Greenbank would close, Yusuf's job would go, and I'd be too slow to catch up because I'm someone who waits to see. What would help is a grant for co-ops to buy shared machines and a basic income or something like it while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but if a robot does the lambing, who notices the ewe that's off her food before she goes down? I'm not sure a machine would, and I'd want someone to check.

headlineQuote: We've survived foot rot, two droughts and a bank manager called Gerhard, so we can survive a robot if we plan.
portrait: Fatima Ibrahim is a 27-year-old member of a small co-op farm with two hundred ewes and a veg box scheme. She lives above the village bakery with her partner Yusuf, a bus driver, with two or three weeks of savings. Progressive and pro-union, she wants co-ops and communities to own the machines. She waits for others to prove new tools before adopting them, which makes her calm at a plateau and steady change but alarmed at AGI in two years, when she fears her careful pace is too slow. With five or ten years she plans an evening course in farm machinery and expects her fear to turn into planning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most: the co-op would close, her partner's bus job would go, and her habit of waiting to see would leave her too slow to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: She'd want grants for co-ops to buy shared machines, and a basic income or similar support while people retrain.
